title: The other two verb groups
goal: Use the remaining two verb groups (*-ę / -esz* and *-ę / -isz*), recognize verbs ending in *-ować*, and talk about your plans for tonight.
bekal: conjugate *-ę / -esz* and *-ę / -isz* verbs for all six persons

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Co robisz dziś wieczorem?
dialogs.intro: The dorm kitchen, late afternoon. Ania is standing at the stove; Budi has just come back from class.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Jeszcze nie wiem. Może idę do kina. A ty?
lines.id: I don't know yet. Maybe I'll go to the cinema. And you?
lines.literal: still not I-know. maybe I-go to cinema. and you?

lines.speaker: Ania:
lines.text: Piszę e-mail do mamy, a potem gotuję kolację.
lines.id: I'm writing an email to my mom, and then I'm cooking dinner.
lines.literal: I-write e-mail to mom, and then I-cook dinner.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Bardzo lubię! Ale nie umiem gotować.
lines.id: I love them! But I can't cook.
lines.literal: very I-like! but not I-know-how cook.

lines.speaker: Ania:
lines.id: It's easy. I'll teach you tomorrow.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Pomagam ci, a ty mówisz, co robić.
lines.id: I'll help you, and you tell me what to do.
lines.literal: I-help to-you, and you say, what do.

lines.speaker: Ania:
lines.text: Umowa. Tylko nie mów mojej mamie — ona myśli, że gotuję źle.
lines.id: Deal. Just don't tell my mom — she thinks I'm a bad cook.
lines.literal: deal. only don't say my mom — she thinks, that I-cook badly.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Nie wierzę. Na pewno gotujesz dobrze.
lines.id: I don't believe it. I'm sure you cook well.

lines.speaker: Ania:
lines.text: Zobaczymy. Teraz idę do sklepu — brakuje mi mąki.
lines.id: We'll see. Now I'm going to the shop — I'm out of flour.
lines.literal: we-will-see. now I-go to shop — lacks to-me flour.

notes: **Dziś wieczorem** — "tonight". *Wieczór* (evening) becomes *wieczorem* to say **when**. The same pattern: *rano* (in the morning), *w południe* (at noon), *w nocy* (at night).

**Idę do kina, idę do sklepu.** The word *do* means "to" and is always followed by a noun form ending in *-a* or *-u*. That form is called *dopełniacz* and is covered fully in Unit 14. For now, just memorize three chunks: *do kina*, *do sklepu*, *do domu*.

**Piszę** comes from *pisać*. Notice: the *s* turns into *sz*. Some *-ę / -esz* verbs do change one letter in the stem. There aren't many, and the common ones can be counted on your fingers — the list is in the extra section of this unit.

**Gotuję from gotować.** All verbs ending in *-ować* change the same way: drop *-ować*, add *-uję, -ujesz, -uje…*. A pleasant group, because the dictionary form tells you right away how to conjugate it.

**Umiem gotować** — the second verb stays in the dictionary form, just like English "I can cook". This pattern works with *umieć* (know how to), *chcieć* (want), *móc* (can), *musieć* (must) — all in Unit 13.
**Uczę cię** — "I teach you". Compare *uczę się* (I learn) from Unit 2. The small word after the verb decides who is being taught.

**Mówisz mi, pomagam ci** — the forms "to me" and "to you" (*mi*, *ci*). This form is called *celownik*, and at A1 you only need four words: *mi* (to me), *ci* (to you), *mu* (to him), *jej* (to her).

**Że** means "that" and is **required**. English can drop it ("she thinks I'm a bad cook"); Polish can't: *ona myśli, że gotuję źle*. Notice the comma before *że* too — in Polish that comma is a rule, not a matter of taste.

grammars.title: Group I: -ę / -esz
body: The mark of this group: the *ja* form ends in **-ę**, the *ty* form in **-esz**. The endings stay fixed; what sometimes changes is the last letter of the stem.
after: Look at the *iść* column: the *ja* and *oni* forms use *id-*, while the four middle forms use *idzi-*. This change of consonant before the ending *-e* is very typical of Polish; it happens because the *e* sound softens the letter before it.

**A shortcut that really works:** learn every new verb in **two forms** — *ja* and *ty*. From those two, the other four can be built without ever going wrong: take the *ty* form minus *-sz* plus *-my* / *-cie*, and the *ja* form minus *-ę* plus *-ą*.
*-ować* verbs are never a problem: *pracować → pracuję*, *studiować → studiuję*, *kupować → kupuję*, *dziękować → dziękuję*. (*Rozmawiać* is not one of them — that's Group III.)

grammars.title: Group II: -ę / -isz
body: The *ja* form also ends in *-ę*, but the *ty* form uses **-isz** (or **-ysz** after a hard consonant). This group contains many of the most common everyday verbs.
after: After *cz*, *sz*, *ż*, *rz*, *j* the endings are spelled **-ysz, -y, -ymy, -ycie**: *uczyć → uczę, uczysz, uczy*. The sound is the same; only the spelling adjusts to the rule that *i* is not written after a hard consonant.

⚠️ Groups II and III are the easiest to mix up, because their *ja* forms differ while the meanings are often similar: *robię* (Group II) but *czytam* (Group III). There's no way to guess from the meaning — always learn the *ja* and *ty* forms along with a new word.

sections.title: The three groups side by side

blocks.text: Every Polish verb fits into one of these three columns. This page is worth bookmarking — you'll come back to it again and again.

head: I: *-ę / -esz*
II: *-ę / -isz*
III: *-am / -asz*
rows: *iść, pisać, pić, brać, gotować, kupować, pracować*
*mówić, robić, lubić, myśleć, uczyć, płacić, widzieć*

blocks.title: Patterns that hold in all three groups
items: The **ja** form always ends in *-m* or *-ę*. There's no third option.
The **ty** form always ends in *-sz*. No exceptions.
The **my** form always ends in *-my*, the **wy** form always in *-cie*.
The **on/ona** form is always the shortest in its column.
These four patterns hold for every Polish verb except *być* — and even *być* follows three of the four.

blocks.text: Some Group I verbs swap one consonant at the end of the stem. This list covers the most common ones; the rest can wait.

All these changes have the same cause: the *e* and *i* sounds in the ending **soften** the letter before them, and Polish writes that softening with a different letter. You don't need to memorize the reason — just recognize that two forms that look different (*idę / idziesz*) really are one and the same word.

blocks.title: Likes and dislikes
items: *Lubię kawę.* — I like coffee. *Nie lubię kawy.* — I don't like coffee.
Notice the ending changes when negated: *kawę* becomes *kawy*. That's a big rule waiting in Unit 14; just recognize the form for now.
*Bardzo lubię…* (I really like) · *Nie znoszę…* (I can't stand) · *Wolę kawę niż herbatę.* (I prefer coffee to tea)
